name: Heap / top-k
plain: A heap (priority queue) is a bag that always hands you its smallest (or largest) item in O(log n). Two jobs it does perfectly: (1) keep only the k best items seen so far — hold a heap of size k, and whenever a new item beats the worst one in the heap, swap it in; (2) repeatedly pick 'the next smallest across many sources' — merging k sorted lists, or scheduling whichever task is available earliest.
whenToUse: you hear 'k largest / smallest / most frequent / closest', 'merge k sorted…', 'median of a stream', or a simulation where you repeatedly need the earliest / cheapest / smallest item among many that keep arriving.
invariant: For top-k: the heap holds exactly the k best items among everything processed so far, with the worst of them at the top. For k-way merge: the heap holds exactly one candidate (the current head) from each still-unfinished source, so the top is the global next item. Both invariants are restored with one push and/or one pop per element.
oneLiner: Keep a small heap of the k best so far (worst one on top, so it is cheap to evict) — or a heap of one head per source, popping the global minimum each time.
intuition:
## Top-k: why the heap is the *opposite* of what you want

To keep the k **largest**, use a **min**-heap. The top is the *smallest of the k largest* — the one that should be evicted if something bigger arrives. With a size-k min-heap, each of n items costs O(log k), total O(n log k), and memory O(k). Sorting everything is O(n log n) and needs all n in memory; the heap works on a stream.

## When k is close to n

If k ≈ n, `nth_element` (quickselect) is O(n) average and beats the heap. If k is tiny, the heap wins. If you need the k items *in order*, you sort the k at the end for O(k log k) extra.

## k-way merge

Merging k sorted lists of total length N: the heap holds the current front of each list (k items). Pop the smallest, push the popped list's next element. N pops × O(log k). The same shape handles 'k-th smallest in a sorted matrix' (rows are the lists) and 'smallest range covering elements from k lists'.

## Two heaps for the running median

A max-heap for the lower half, a min-heap for the upper half, sizes differing by at most 1. The median is one or both tops. Each insertion: push to one side, then rebalance by moving one top across. The invariant 'every element in low ≤ every element in high' is what you must protect.

## Scheduling simulations

Meeting Rooms II, Task Scheduler, CPU scheduling: sort events by start, keep a heap of 'when does each running thing finish'. Before starting a new one, pop everything that has finished. The heap answers 'what frees up earliest?' in O(log n).

## Recognising it

The word **k** together with best/worst; the word **stream** or 'online'; **many sorted sources**; a **simulation** that repeatedly asks for the earliest/cheapest of a changing set.
workedExample:
## Kth Largest Element: `nums = [3,2,1,5,6,4]`, k = 2 → answer 5

Min-heap of size 2. Push; if size > k, pop the smallest.

| x | after push | pop? | heap (min on left) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | [3] | no | [3] |
| 2 | [2,3] | no | [2,3] |
| 1 | [1,2,3] | pop 1 | [2,3] |
| 5 | [2,3,5] | pop 2 | [3,5] |
| 6 | [3,5,6] | pop 3 | [5,6] |
| 4 | [4,5,6] | pop 4 | [5,6] |

Top of the heap = 5 = the 2nd largest. The heap never held more than 3 items.

**Boundary check:** k = n → the heap holds everything, top is the minimum = n-th largest. k = 1 → heap of size 1 always holds the max seen so far.

## Merge k Sorted Lists: `[1,4,5], [1,3,4], [2,6]`

Heap holds (value, listIndex). Start: {(1,0), (1,1), (2,2)}.

| pop | output so far | push (next of that list) | heap |
|---|---|---|---|
| (1,0) | 1 | (4,0) | (1,1) (2,2) (4,0) |
| (1,1) | 1 1 | (3,1) | (2,2) (3,1) (4,0) |
| (2,2) | 1 1 2 | (6,2) | (3,1) (4,0) (6,2) |
| (3,1) | 1 1 2 3 | (4,1) | (4,0) (4,1) (6,2) |
| (4,0) | … 4 | (5,0) | (4,1) (5,0) (6,2) |
| (4,1) | … 4 | — (list 1 done) | (5,0) (6,2) |
| (5,0) | … 5 | — | (6,2) |
| (6,2) | … 6 | — | ∅ |

Every element is pushed once and popped once: O(N log k).
templateNotes: `priority_queue` in C++ is a **max**-heap by default; pass `greater<>` for a min-heap. Saying out loud 'I need the *worst of the best* on top, so a min-heap for largest' prevents the most common bug in this pattern.

canonical.title: Kth Largest Element in an Array

twists: **Sorted matrix** (Kth Smallest in a Sorted Matrix): rows are the k sorted sources; push (val, row, col), pop k times. Or binary-search on the answer with a 'count ≤ x' check — both are valid, say which and why.

**Lazy deletion** (Sliding Window Median, task scheduling with cancellations): a heap cannot delete arbitrary items — push a tombstone or keep a 'to remove' map and discard stale tops when they surface.
**Heap of k=1 is just a max**: if the interviewer's k becomes 1, drop the heap and keep a variable — showing you notice this is worth points.
**Frequency reorganisation** (Reorganize String, Task Scheduler): a max-heap on remaining counts; pop the most frequent that is not the one you just placed, then push it back with count-1.
**Weighted 'closest'** (K Closest Points): the key is the distance, the payload is the point — store a pair and compare on the key only.
followups: What if k is close to n — is the heap still the right tool?
The data is a stream that never ends; what is your memory footprint?
How would you remove an element that is no longer valid from the middle of the heap?
Can you return the k items in sorted order, and what does that cost?
pitfalls: Using a max-heap for 'k largest' and popping k times — O(n log n) memory-heavy, and evicting the wrong end when you try to cap size.
Comparing pairs where the payload participates in the ordering unintentionally (ties broken by value when the problem says 'any order').
Forgetting that `std::priority_queue` has no decrease-key — use lazy deletion or `std::set` if you genuinely need it.
In the two-heap median, letting the halves drift by 2 — rebalance after **every** insertion.
